Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Police officers responsible for protecting the British royal family handled firearms when drunk, traded pornography and steroids and sat on Queen Elizabeth II's throne in comical poses, it has been alleged in a London court. The former royal protection officer was responsible for security at Buckingham Palace. The allegations were made Tuesday by John Cooper, the lawyer for former royal protection officer Paul Page, who is accused of defrauding colleagues and friends to fund a life of luxury, The British Press Association reported. According to PA, the claims were made during a lengthy cross-examination of Adam McGregor, a colleague of Page who left service at London's Buckingham Palace in 2005, who has accused the former officer of "conning" him out of thousands of dollars. At one point Cooper "suggested" there had been a procedure among armed officers at the palace whereby one officer on duty would sleep while the others kept watch for their superior. McGregor denied any knowledge of this and all other allegations of wrongdoing among his colleagues at the iconic Royal residence. However, when pressed further he did admit to sitting on one of the thrones, but did not recall doing any "comical poses." The court also heard that officers protecting the royals lost more than £250,000 ($365,800) to a spread betting venture called "The Currency Club," one of a number of apparently successful sidelines Page allegedly set up to clear spiraling debts, PA said. According to the BBC, Page extracted around £3 million ($4.4 million) from some 57 lenders or investors. Cooper suggested that McGregor had been "one of those police officers" using mobile patrols to deliver cash to other police officers based in Royal Protection who were involved in financial matters. The accusation was again denied by McGregor. He instead claimed he had been "totally sucked in" by Page. "I was totally sucked in by Paul he is a very charismatic person," he said, before adding that he had acted "very naively and very stupidly" in some of his dealings with his former colleague. The prosecution claimed much of the money was promptly laundered by Page's wife before being gambled away, as Page himself hid his dishonesty behind a " veneer of credibility" fueled by a fleet of expensive cars and claims he was a highly "adept" property developer and market speculator, PA said. Father of five Page, 37, from Essex in south-east England, has denied five charges -- two of fraudulent trading, one of intimidation, threatening to take revenge and making a threat to kill between January 1, 2003 and March 30, 2007. His wife Laura, 42, denied "being concerned in an arrangement facilitating dealings with criminal property," intimidation and threatening to kill.

As England's capital, London also plays a central role in the country's political discourse, with Westminster serving as the site of Parliament and the seat of government. Decisions made within its walls ripple far beyond the city limits, affecting policy across the UK and often influencing international relations.

Looking ahead, London faces the dual task of preserving its rich heritage while continuing to innovate in sectors such as technology, green energy, and finance. Analysts suggest that the city's ability to balance tradition with progress will likely determine its trajectory in an increasingly interconnected and rapidly changing world.

**LONDON** — A former member of the royal protection squad appeared in court this week as prosecutors laid out a case alleging years of fraud, witness intimidation, and threatening behavior that they say was enabled by his previous position of trust guarding the British royal family.

Paul Page, who served in the specialist unit tasked with protecting senior royals before leaving the role under circumstances now central to the prosecution's case, faces multiple charges including fraud by false representation, intimidation of witnesses, and making threats against individuals connected to the investigation.

## Prosecution Lays Out Timeline

Prosecutors told the court that Page allegedly leveraged his former royal connections and insider knowledge to establish credibility for a series of business dealings that later unraveled into what they characterize as a sustained fraud scheme. The prosecution argued that Page's background gave him an air of authority that he used to convince associates and investors to trust him with funds and sensitive arrangements.

The court heard that when suspicions began to surface among those allegedly defrauded, Page turned to intimidation tactics — including direct threats and efforts to silence people who might cooperate with authorities.

## Witness Cross-Examination Reveals Tensions

During cross-examination this week, defense counsel repeatedly challenged the reliability and motivations of prosecution witnesses, several of whom acknowledged under questioning that they had ongoing financial disputes with Page predating the alleged offenses.

One witness, giving evidence from behind a screen, described receiving a series of phone calls he characterized as menacing after he raised questions about missing funds. Under cross-examination, the defense pressed the witness on inconsistencies between his police statement and his testimony in court, at one point suggesting that his account had "evolved considerably" since the initial complaint was filed. The witness maintained that any discrepancies were the product of trauma and fear rather than fabrication.

Another witness, a former business associate of Page's, testified that he had felt unable to go to police earlier because of what he described as veiled threats referencing Page's "connections." Defense counsel countered by highlighting the witness's own financial troubles at the time, suggesting a possible motive to falsely implicate the defendant. The witness firmly denied any ulterior motive, insisting, "I said nothing until I felt I had no choice."

The defense also focused on the timeline of events, pointing out gaps between when alleged threats were said to have occurred and when they were formally reported to police — a delay the defense argued cast doubt on the credibility of the claims.

## Defense Strategy Takes Shape

Page's legal team has signaled it intends to argue that the prosecution's case relies heavily on witnesses with credibility issues and financial motives of their own, rather than solid documentary evidence. Defense counsel has suggested that ordinary business disputes have been recast as criminal conduct by parties seeking to avoid their own obligations or settle personal scores.

The prosecution, meanwhile, maintains that the pattern of behavior — moving from alleged financial deception to alleged coercion once questions arose — points to a deliberate and calculated scheme rather than a series of unfortunate misunderstandings.

## What Comes Next

The trial is expected to continue in the coming weeks, with additional witnesses, including individuals who worked alongside Page during and after his time in royal protection duties, expected to be called to testify. The case has drawn significant public attention given Page's former role safeguarding some of the most protected figures in the United Kingdom — a position prosecutors say makes the allegations against him all the more striking.
